question: "I make all things new." What actually happens at the end?
intro: Revelation ends with God saying He'll make everything new. No more death, no more tears. Most people either skip Revelation because it's weird or obsess over it because it's weird. The end of the plan of salvation is the part that's supposed to make the middle worth it. So what actually happens? Judgment, kingdoms, a new earth. Preach My Gospel covers it in a page. This week we take the page seriously.

days.q: What does John see at the end?
days.intro: Read the last two chapters of Revelation. New heaven, new earth, no more sea, no more death. God with people, not far from them. When you read, notice what's gone and what's left. The list of what's gone is specific.
days.journal: Revelation 21:4 says God will wipe away all tears. What's the tear you most want wiped away? Write it down.

days.q: What did the prophets before John see?
days.intro: John wasn't the first. Isaiah saw a new heaven and a new earth seven centuries earlier, and he saw the wolf and the lamb together. Apocalyptic writing used pictures because the thing was too big for plain words. Read Isaiah, then read Jesus describing the same thing as a house with many mansions.
days.journal: Isaiah says the former things won't be remembered or come to mind. Is there a former thing you're not sure you'd want to forget? Why?

days.q: What did Joseph Smith see?
days.intro: D&C 76 is the most detailed description of the afterlife anywhere in scripture. Three kingdoms, described in order from lowest to highest. Read the telestial and terrestrial first, because they're more generous than most people expect, then the celestial. When you read, look for who ends up where and why.
days.journal: D&C 76:89 says the glory of the *lowest* kingdom surpasses all understanding. What does that tell you about God's plan for people who reject Him?

days.q: What does an apostle say about the kingdoms?
days.intro: President Dallin H. Oaks, October 2023. He explains the three kingdoms plainly and says why the doctrine should change how you live now.
days.takeaway: His point is that the doctrine of three kingdoms is the most merciful thing in Christianity. Almost everyone ends up in a kingdom of glory. The question isn't heaven or hell, it's how much of God you want to be around, and He gives you exactly what you're willing to receive. Oaks says the celestial kingdom is for people who want to live with God's *laws*, not just His presence, and the difference matters for what you choose today.
days.journal: Oaks says God gives you what you're willing to receive. What are you willing to receive right now? Be honest about the ceiling you've set.

days.q: Is anyone actually lost?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. Three kingdoms of glory sounds like everybody wins. So what about judgment? What about hell? Read the sons of perdition, the only people D&C 76 says are lost, and notice how narrow that is. Then read D&C 19, where the Lord explains what "endless punishment" actually means, and it's not what you think. Then Alma on restoration: you get back what you sent.
days.journal: Alma says you'll be restored to what you actually were. Not what you said you were. If that happened today, what would you be restored to?

days.q: How do you live like the end is real?
days.intro: Jesus told a story about ten bridesmaids and half of them weren't ready. The Lord says stand in holy places and don't be moved. He says if you're prepared you won't fear. When you read, look for what being ready actually involves. It's not stockpiling. It's something else.
days.journal: The five wise virgins had oil they couldn't share. What's your oil? What have you actually stored up this year that nobody can give you?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Back to Revelation 21. Read verses 3 through 5 one more time. Then read your Day 1 tear and what you wrote in Week 25 about resurrection.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: What actually happens at the end? And what does that make you want to do with the next year?

question: Christmas. Why a baby? Why a manger? Why then?
intro: God came to earth. He could have come any way He wanted. Fire on a mountain, a king in a palace, a warrior in the sky. He came as a baby to a teenager in a town nobody cared about, and they put Him in a feeding trough. None of that was an accident. This week is Christmas, and the question is why He did it the way He did it. Nephi called it the condescension of God. Let's find out what that means.

days.q: What does Luke say happened?
days.intro: Read the Christmas story like you've never heard it. Census, no room, shepherds, angels. When you read, notice how ordinary the first half is and how loud the second half gets. Then read Matthew's version, which is darker and has a king trying to kill the baby.
days.journal: What part of the Christmas story do you actually think about, and what part do you skip? Write it down.

days.q: Why Bethlehem, and why a manger?
days.intro: Bethlehem means "house of bread." Micah named it as the Messiah's birthplace 700 years early. It was David's town. The shepherds nearby raised lambs for the temple sacrifices, which means the first people to see the Lamb of God were the guys who raised the lambs. And a manger is a feeding trough. The Bread of Life was laid in a place where animals eat. Read the prophecies and then the story again.
days.journal: The first witnesses were shepherds who raised sacrificial lambs. God picks His audience on purpose. Who's the audience He picked for you this year?

days.q: What did the Book of Mormon see?
days.intro: Nephi saw the birth 600 years before it happened and an angel asked him if he understood the condescension of God. He said no. Then he saw a virgin with a baby. Alma described it to a city that didn't want to hear it. Samuel gave the sign. And then read the night it actually happened on this continent, with people about to be executed for believing it.
days.journal: 3 Nephi 1:13: "on the morrow come I into the world." The Savior said that the night before He was born. What do you feel reading that?

days.q: What does an apostle say about why He came that way?
days.intro: Elder Jeffrey R. Holland, October 2003. He gave a talk on what Jesus came to show us about the Father, and the birth is the start of it.
days.takeaway: His point is that Jesus came to show us what God is actually like, because we'd gotten it wrong. Every time Jesus fed someone, healed someone, forgave someone, He was saying: this is my Father. Holland says the baby in the manger was the Father's way of introducing Himself, and if you want to know what God thinks of you, look at how His Son treated people.
days.journal: Holland says Jesus came to show us the Father. What's one thing about God you only know because of something Jesus did?

days.q: Why so ordinary?
days.intro: Here's the hard part. He could have come in glory and settled every argument. Instead He came so quietly that almost nobody noticed, in a body that Isaiah says had no beauty that we should desire Him. Why? Read Paul on what Christ gave up. Read Isaiah on what He looked like. Read Nephi's word again: condescension. Then decide why God chose small.
days.journal: He chose to come small and unnoticed. What does that tell you about how He might be showing up in your life, and how you might be missing it?

days.q: What do you give Him?
days.intro: The wise men brought gifts. King Benjamin gave a sermon about the coming Christ and then told his people what to do with it. The Savior Himself said what He wants, and it's not gold. When you read, look for what you actually have that He'd want.
read: Preach My Gospel, lesson 1, "Jesus Christ's Earthly Ministry and Atonement"
days.journal: What's your gift this Christmas? Not the ones under the tree. The one you'd give Him. Write it, then figure out how to actually give it this week.

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: Christmas week. Read the shepherds one more time, and then read Nephi's answer to the angel.
days.journal: Answer the week's question: Why a baby? Why a manger? Why then? Say it the way you'd tell it to your family on Christmas Eve.

question: What do I believe now?
intro: Fifty-one weeks. Fifty-one questions. Every week you ended by writing what you believe. This week you read all of it back. Not to grade yourself. To see what a year of asking hard questions did to you. Some of your answers will surprise you. Some you'll disagree with now. That's the point. By Day 7 you'll write one thing: what you believe. In your own words. Nobody else's.

days.q: Where did you start?
days.intro: Read your Day 7 answers from the first eight weeks. Waiting on God, baptism, fasting, being perfect, prayer, being born again, being called, faith. Read them in order. When you read, notice which ones you'd write differently now.
days.journal: Which of these eight would you rewrite today? Why?

days.q: What did the Savior's ministry teach you?
days.intro: Weeks 9 through 17. Worry, healing, repentance, parables, Easter, Peter on the water, revelation, forgiveness, the Samaritan. Read your answers. When you read, look for a thread. Something you kept coming back to without meaning to.
days.journal: What's the thread? What kept showing up in your answers that you didn't plan?

days.q: What did the last week of His life teach you?
days.intro: Weeks 18 through 26. The older brother, the rich young man, the temple, the Book of Mormon, the last night, Gethsemane, the cross, resurrection, the Holy Ghost. Read them. When you read, notice which answer you're proudest of and which one you're least sure of.
days.journal: Which answer are you least sure of now? What would it take to be sure?

days.q: What did the early Church teach you?
days.intro: Weeks 27 through 35. Saul, Peter's vision, your conference talk, grace, why you're here, charity, not knowing, the dead, thorns. Read them. When you read, look for the one that changed how you actually act, not just what you think.
days.journal: Which week actually changed what you do? What's different because of it?

days.q: What did the epistles teach you?
days.intro: Weeks 36 through 44. The Spirit, apostles, strength, enduring, apostasy, your second conference talk, learning through suffering, priesthood, faith and works. Read them. When you read, notice whether your answers got shorter or longer over the year, and what that means.
days.journal: Did your answers get more sure or less sure as the year went on? Is that good?

days.q: What did the end teach you?
days.intro: Weeks 45 through 51. James 1:5, becoming like God, the Fall, the Lamb, the war in heaven, the end, Christmas. Read them. Then read Alma's questions, which are the questions this whole year was asking.
days.journal: Alma 5:26: if you've felt to sing the song of redeeming love, can you feel so now? Can you?

days.q: What do I believe now?
days.intro: No reading today except three verses and your own year. Nephi's instruction for what to do next. Moroni's promise about what Christ does with you. Then write. Not a testimony you've heard before. Yours. What you actually believe, after a year of asking. Write it like it's the only thing anyone will ever read from you.
days.journal: What do you believe? Write it. Then read it out loud to someone this week.
